claims.text: Conventionally cast or slowly cooled refractory high-entropy alloys have relatively coarse, equilibrium grain structures.
The untreated alloy typically combines high strength and impact-induced energy release with limited ductility.
Rapid solidification will refine the alloy microstructure.
Controlled low-temperature annealing after rapid solidification will stabilize a nanostructured grain-boundary network.
The treatment will produce grain boundaries with improved distribution and coherency.
The resulting nanostructured grain-boundary network will mediate dislocation motion and plasticity.
Nanostructured grain boundaries will increase the number of obstacles associated with dislocation pile-up.
The altered interaction between grain boundaries and dislocations will promote a more uniform strain distribution.
The refined microstructure will delay localized failure.
Rapid solidification followed by low-temperature annealing will increase elongation to failure and uniform deformability relative to the conventionally processed control.
The treatment will cause no more than a modest reduction in yield strength.
Impact-induced energy release after treatment will remain similar to, or within 5% of, the untreated baseline.
The beneficial effects should hold from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures under quasi-static and impact testing conditions.
The beneficial effects may not hold at very high temperatures, extreme strain rates, or in corrosive atmospheres.
A statistically significant 10–20% increase in elongation to failure is the proposed minimum ductility improvement.
A yield-strength decrease greater than approximately 5%, when accompanied by compromised impact energy release, is proposed as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires strength preservation with at most a modest reduction, but the falsification rule does not make a yield-strength loss above 5% independently falsifying; it requires that loss to occur together with compromised impact performance.

The hypothesis predicts retention of impact-induced energy release, whereas the experiment lists impact energy absorption and labels it as energy release. Energy absorption and energetic-material energy release are not necessarily equivalent observables.
